### The default test run runs inline again, never as a verification job, and a passed run is recorded for the push and release gates

[`1ba6d2ed715c`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/1ba6d2ed715c2904ed95251654c87de604d76406) · [log `4cea52ec32b4`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/4cea52ec32b474e38d481508fb9fd1cab080db066f03c25be70249bb4da9e228.jsonl.gz)

The user decided to take the default run out of the verification pipeline: as a job it overlapped other runs in one cargo target directory (VF-034), was cut off with its runner at the Bash tool's 10-minute limit, and skipped the one-at-a-time lock when queued from a line that predated it. verification/default_tests.py (queue, step, supersede, bisect, the unread-file list, flaky counts) and its tests are removed, with verification/default-tests-unread.txt and the watcher's default-tests event.

New lib/tools/default_run.py: a whole default run (test_costs.py run) that passes records the git tree it tested, as jj snapshots the working copy, and only when no file changed during the run, in ~/.cache/in-the-loop/default-runs.jsonl. At the user's word after the first /run-brief rehearsal (2026-11-17), whose merge loop took the finished streams for empty because their notes were not in its working copy's files, and in which a finished stream waited for the slowest. run-streams.sh now puts each finished stream, done or left blocked, to the watcher at once (conductor.py's new merge question, RUN_STREAMS_MERGE_WAIT, 30 min), while the others still run, and no longer runs the brief's own loop after the streams; a brief without streams still runs as its own loop, now labelled brief. brief_run.py merge BRIEF STREAM merges the stream's @- into the default line as land does, takes its session logs (land now runs sync.py adopt-logs too) and inbox acknowledgements, answers the question merged, records the merge in the brief's Progress (status done once every stream is merged and done, blocked: stream S: ... when one was left blocked) and commits it with the decision; it commits the run's own decision record first, so the watcher's earlier answers don't block it, and run again after a hand-made merge it only records it. ### The watcher of a brief's run collects and commits verification results itself, and landing drops trace output left uncommitted

[`f5d19330ec3f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/f5d19330ec3f13b22638743e997de08e7ef88c09) · [log `da5a0a03ac92`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/da5a0a03ac92bb24cbe31f40b395cf3621e86910e7549ee7afce8fea0c0f8baa.jsonl.gz)

With a watcher, run-streams.sh starts no verification loop. At each look at the queue, brief_run.py wait collects the results that are back and commits them with --only the paths pipeline.py commit-paths names, starts the runner (pipeline.py run, no model) when jobs wait and none is at work, and records the inbox items the streams' committed Progress acknowledges. It returns a 'results' event with the jobs to triage in 'attention'; the watcher triages them as the run-verification skill says. brief_run.py collect does the same by hand, for the report. A verification loop already running keeps the queue as before. Merges and collections take turns by a lock, so the watcher is the one session committing in the default working copy while a run is under way.

land (and so merge) now treats uncommitted trace output (llm-dlc/traces/, llm-dlc/index.json, the decision views, and llm-dlc/README.md when only its session table changed) as nobody's work: it is dropped, not waited for and not carried onto the other line, and the next sync.py run writes it again. In the rehearsal it was there after the foundation landed, and a second real-time merge would have waited for a commit no session was going to make. A move forward that makes another session's uncommitted files conflict is taken back; the jj steps hold sync.py's repository lock; the precise list of generated paths replaces the 'llm-dlc/ or README.md' prefix that sent any file under llm-dlc/ written during a merge into the merge commit.

### A proof by induction and a lemma's summary no longer stand in for a call that writes, throws, or reads what a caller can change

[`1b724784543f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/1b724784543f7da41ef5b56ec9b7e722c816f24a) · [log `485da70bcb76`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/485da70bcb765170eb169d2834f50fdf1093d602f220c87e50df7d8c472f72e1.jsonl.gz)

Three false proofs, each reproduced first on the checker as it was (lib/tests/fixtures/claims/claims/Effects.java, whose main prints what a JVM says): (1) prove --decreases on a method that counts its calls in a static field proved 'result == 1' where a JVM returns 2, because the induction hypothesis replaced the inner call and dropped its write; (2) with a throws clause, the hypothesis returned a value for an inner call the property itself says throws, and proved 'result == n' of a method that never returns; (3) a lemma about a getter, proved in the fresh state where its static field is 0, was used as a summary after the caller wrote the field, and proved 'result == 0' of a method that returns what it wrote. The same held through a callee, through an array a static field holds, for the default locale, and for a lemma whose own assertion reads a field.

Now: a method proved by induction is held to the write checks a summary's method already had (Options::own_induction says the proof is by induction alone, where reads are sound because the inner calls are made in the state of the call under proof); the hypothesis does not cover arguments on which a throws clause says the call throws (the induction then does not go through); a lemma's method, and the lemma's assumption and assertion, may read no static field that is not final, no non-final field or cell of an object that was there before the call, and not the default locale (Engine::reads); a summary is not used while its method's class is still being initialized. A lemma about a method of no parameters now compiles (its assertion is over the result alone).

Which existing results rest on these mechanisms: none uses prove --decreases directly; examples 286 and 288 use lemmas about PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch(String,String), whose bytecode in the pinned 5.3.19 JAR reads no field and no array (javap), so their results did not rest on the hole; that the tightened checks still prove those lemmas is for a job to confirm. Verified by lib/tests/claims.rs (18 passed, among them the three new tests and the changed lemma test: a method that counts with calls++ is now refused at its read, one that only writes at its write), the summary unit tests, and test_costs.py run --changed (8 of 8 passed: cargo test's 33 binaries and three Python files).

### A write set, a first effect contract: prove --writes refutes the setter that writes a protected field and proves its honest twin

[`dfb25346d236`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/dfb25346d2367b9ce36946b5ca6fba175f5e0cf0) · [log `7de4b3febd42`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/7de4b3febd42fe99ceaea595e8e37689a68f198f2c0cc4ce161cfe542c719078.jsonl.gz)

The state stream's steps 4 and 5, the checking side. prove --writes this.displayName (own checker only) states which fields of a method's receiver and object parameters it may write. The check proves the frame with the property: after a normal return every other field of those inputs is unchanged, a primitive by value and a String or object by identity through the new p == \old(p) term. The frame is conjoined to the assertion, so a write outside the set is refuted by the harness and its witness runs on a JVM. Inside the call the engine refuses, by name, a write to anything else that existed before it: a static field, an array, an object no input is (even one a named field holds), or a class initialization, whose objects would look new to the call. This generalizes Engine::keeps through bmc::Options::frame. The cache refuses such a check, since its key does not read the write set.

### A write set's frame holds on a declared exceptional exit and is of locations over inputs that may be one object: the challenge stream's three false frames are refuted or proved as JML's assignable states them

[`071fde146465`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/071fde14646550e4042207bec363871cbd798f9a) · [log `7de4b3febd42`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/7de4b3febd42fe99ceaea595e8e37689a68f198f2c0cc4ce161cfe542c719078.jsonl.gz)

Inbox item domain-advances-state-I005 (the challenge stream's countermodels, synvlnls, fc.Framed). Before this commit, prove --writes proved a frame in two cases where a JVM sees the protected field written. In the first, a method writes admin and then throws an exception its throws clause declares: the frame was part of the assertion, which was read only after a normal return. The harness now checks the frame after the expected exception too (harness::generate_property_framed, whose \old reads take their own locals after the assertion's), so rename("b", -1) is refuted with a witness a JVM replays. In the second, one bean is passed as two inputs. The frame is now of locations, as JML's assignable is. Every two inputs of one class may be one object: the check adds the alias choice, and the domain says so. A field that one of them names is framed in the other only where the two differ (this == other || this.admin == \old(this.admin)). So promote --writes other.admin and grant --writes to.admin are proved with that frame, which a JVM keeps, and never with the unaliased one, which it breaks. A write set with a construction plan over two inputs of one class is refused by name. Where a witness throws a declared exception over objects, its expected line now names the frame instead of wrongly saying 'a normal return'.

Tests. lib/tests/fixtures/frame-countermodels (README and fc/Framed.java) and the JVM test in lib/tests/frame_countermodels.rs are copied unchanged from synvlnls. The README's checker-side test a_write_set_is_not_proved_where_a_jvm_sees_a_field_it_does_not_name_written is added, adapted to the location frame: rename must be refuted with a JVM replay, and promote and grant must not prove the unaliased frame. The README's version required those two not to be Verified, which none of the options it lists for aliasing (a location frame, or distinct objects in the domain) would give. A second test proves that what the frame names is allowed on either exit and alias. ### A library method the own checker can't run may be replaced by a stand-in sampled against it on a JVM (prove --stand-in), and a result that used one says it rests on it

[`cc50b5aaf171`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/cc50b5aaf1713192a9250970a51a8cd821d20901) · [log `7de4b3febd42`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/7de4b3febd42fe99ceaea595e8e37689a68f198f2c0cc4ce161cfe542c719078.jsonl.gz)

Step 3, option 2, of the state stream's brief. Spring's bean wrapper resolves a property through its introspection caches and java.beans and calls the setter with Method.invoke, on every path of DataBinder.bind (example 286). Observing those caches is refused, and running them would need models of java.beans and java.lang.reflect. So the binding path gets a stand-in instead. Each public static method of the stand-in class (but main) replaces an instance method: its first parameter's class is the exact class of the receivers it covers, the rest of its descriptor is the method's. A call resolving to that method on a receiver of exactly that class runs the stand-in. A subclass's receiver, and the stand-in's own calls, run the method as written, so a stand-in hands back what it does not cover. Its main prints one line per sample with the method's outcome and the stand-in's. The tool runs it first on the check's class path and takes the stand-in only if every sample is the same, refusing it by the first input that differs, or when nothing is sampled, or for a public method that replaces nothing. A result that used a stand-in names it among what it rests on, with the number of samples, as sampled evidence and not a proof. A refutation through one is still replayed on a JVM. JBMC and --cache are refused.

Verified by lib/tests/stand_in.rs on the fixture lib/tests/fixtures/stand-ins, a reflective property writer. With the stand-in, a claim the method leaves undecided is proved and the stand-in is named; a refutation replays on a JVM. A subclass receiver, and a bean the stand-in hands back, stop at the method's gap as before. A stand-in that forgets 'Age', one that samples nothing, and one with a public helper are refused. Switching off the exact-receiver check, or the sample comparison, by mutation makes a test fail. test_costs run --changed passes, after the proof cache's projection named the new option. 286's own stand-in is drafted, not committed: sampled against 5.3.19's setPropertyValue, its 38,400 samples all match. Wiring it into the driver is the next cycle. The brief is not out of date.

### A preservation proof is non-vacuous only with a witness outside the allowed change, and accept.py asks the outcome to say so

[`677bfee17743`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/677bfee17743c0ce042029b3e8f788bbc1ebcc84) · [log `30a05ef3c829`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/30a05ef3c829108103c1018da7dce1ad7cbdd94d96d460706bd7d8bae5e7c31f.jsonl.gz)

Step 4 of the evidence stream's brief. A regression check made as a property of the pair of versions (lib/src/pairing.rs, the route of examples 289's and 290's preservation) proves RegressionPair.agree, which returns true on an input inside the allowed change without calling either version. The property check's vacuity probe asked only for an input of the assumption, so it called a proof non-vacuous even when every assumed input lay inside the change. The control: example 289's preservation through its own driver, with only --unchanged-unless replaced by true, was verified and non-vacuous (a capped 5 s probe). 290's recorded witness, servlets=[], lies inside its own allowed change.

The fix: a verified pair with an allowed change is checked once more, meantToChange against result over the same assumption, domain and class path. A proof makes the statement vacuous; a witness, replayed as any is, becomes the statement's, with the new stated.vacuity.outside naming the change. The regression harness's own probe sets outside too, since that harness returns before the probe on an input in the scope. Now the true control is vacuous, 289 with its own change is non-vacuous at servletPath="" (0.3 s more) and 290 at servlets=[0] (capped probes, recorded in both examples' notes). accept.py refuses an establishment of a task with an allowed change whose outcome does not say its witness lies outside that change (unbound) or names another (fail). So 289's and 290's accepted preservation answers are refused until a rerun on a checker with this fix; the other six stay accepted.

Verified: lib/tests/pairing.rs a_pairs_proof_is_vacuous_when_the_allowed_change_covers_every_assumed_input (tool tier, fails without the fix with NonVacuous), three new cases in examples/tools/test_accept.py, the 289 checkout test now expecting preservation refused for this reason; test_costs.py run --changed 8 of 8, estimate, tag and lint clean; validate_example.py 289 and 290 pass. lib/README.md describes the check.

The brief's 'Where it stands' paragraph is out of date: 289's and 290's preservation are refused now, and every accepted answer of 289 and 290 carries no limit about unrecorded artifacts.

examples/307-*/records/step-6-call-level.md is the note and step-6-call-level-probes.json the runs. lib/tests/fixtures/callee-countermodels/prototype-one-function.patch (against kskmpmny, git 10b5d9c0, after prototype-model.patch) names a callee's outcome by the key of the state at its entry, as a loop's state past the bound is named, and checks no side condition. With it, at the claim's frozen parameters and assumption, in capped probes (4 GB, 300 s): with the relation at crypt_raw on JDK 25, preservation is verified in 79 s (878 MB) and the mutant is a violation in 58 s, replayed on a JVM; with it at hashpw(byte[], String), preservation is verified in 53 s on JDK 21 and the run is killed at 4 GB on JDK 25, and the mutant has no verdict under the claim's seven salts (the first candidate has salt = null) and is a violation under one valid salt. Without a relation the runs die at 4 GB.

The JDK 25 difference: hashpw(byte[], String) calls Integer.parseInt, whose bytecode the checker follows, and JDK 25's parseInt(String, int) calls String.format(String, Object[]), which shared::reach takes as a way back into the application since kskmpmny. The fixture gains the row parsed (Parsing.java, a callee that calls Integer.parseInt): verified on JDK 21 and no verdict on JDK 25 on kskmpmny, in under a second.

The prototype against the fixture's rows: by formula it falsely proves wiped and counted (what the callee writes is not in its outcome); with a relation by content added it falsely proves table, seeded, helped and aliased too. No other row turns. So the rows separate a rule with its side conditions from one without.

### Countermodels of a checked summary: seven false proofs past the foundation's refusals, refused

[`569cf0dada85`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/569cf0dada85b815e844bb026f031471163b717f) · [log `2bc94a811e55`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/2bc94a811e5517b9ea26e981a72247c3fa41f654bab6f5ed36a6abd239c1784d.jsonl.gz)

Item 3 of the challenge brief. Seven lemmas were proved and their summaries made the checker prove properties a JVM contradicts (fixtures in lib/tests/fixtures/lemma-countermodels, its README has the table).

The first group is an initializer cycle that calls the lemma's method before the final static field it reads is written (seen and heldSeen: proved 7, a JVM gives 0). The foundation's guard looked only at the method's own class.

The second is a final static whose initializer, run by the lemma's proof in the harness's state, reads what a caller changes before it initializes the class: a static (setThenOwn), the default locale (turkishThenLowered) and another class's array (setThenCopied).

The third is a StringBuilder a final static holds, read by the model directly or through a method reference (appendThenLogged and appendThenLoggedThroughLambda). The model's reads never asked Engine::reads.

Summaries are no stream's this run, so they are refused here (lib/src/bmc/mod.rs, strings.rs). No summary is used while any class is being initialized; the call runs as written, so seen and heldSeen are now violations, as on a JVM. Class initializers a lemma's proof runs are held to the lemma's read gate, and objects there when one starts or returns count as there before the call. A lemma reads no StringBuilder that was there before the call.

Tried and found guarded, each with its guard named in the README: a lambda's captured array, the ArrayList model, reflection, self-recursive and mutual lemmas, Pattern and Matcher, model statics, and an induction measure.

Audit: the only lemma in use is PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch (286, 288). It has no statics or initializer, calls only String methods, and is never called from an initializer, so 286's decided result is not affected.

### Two wrong 5.6.4 matchers satisfy 289's established security and preservation claims: one that sets DOTALL only for a pattern ending in '.*', and one that leaves the query out of the URL

[`ea35ef5f2b87`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/ea35ef5f2b8795a5aa408895bd3d65fecc7917cb) · [log `e19940212105`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/e1994021210567a7d7551a09018df1b4065a84649287788ac5e2e8ce041217f9.jsonl.gz)

Item 6 of the domain-advances challenge brief, for example 289 (CVE-2022-22978, spring-security-web 5.6.3 to 5.6.4). On the claims' family, a literal prefix P followed by '.*', and at bound 8, the security claim and the preservation claim together fix 5.6.4's answer on every input. So a wrong matcher can satisfy both only by differing outside that domain. Two do. Each is a patch of 5.6.4's RegexRequestMatcher.java (blob a334afc7, checked against the sources JAR) under the example's controls/, and no task uses either. controls/dotall-for-trailing-wildcard-only.patch sets DOTALL only where the pattern ends with '.*'. On a JVM it misses '/admin/.*/edit' against /admin/, a line feed, /edit, which is the advisory's bypass for a '.' with more pattern after it. controls/query-dropped.patch matches without the query, so '/files/.*\?download=.*' never matches a download request. Both are predicted established under both claims.

The rule for a call both versions share (lib/src/bmc/ties.rs, lib/src/shared.rs one_function) now takes three more cases. An instance method, where nothing can read its receiver after the call: no live local of any frame (an exception's handler counted), no other stack place, no static field, no other object; the receiver's fields are among the inputs. An array result, where the code returns an array it made of a length it computes from constants and static tables' lengths that is a constant at the call (crypt_raw's new byte[cdata.length * 4]). What a call may write is what it reaches through an argument, the receiver, or a static its code takes other than to copy it at once, so bcrypt's tables, which it only clones, stay inputs. Two cost fixes found by profiling: inputs that are the same formulas are now related without a solver literal, and a check whose first run used the whole budget reports that run rather than an empty fallback.

The challenge stream's seven false proofs of the one-function rule (lib/tests/fixtures/function-countermodels), and an eighth found while reading it, are now refused or refuted. Each was Verified before: filled and copied (a callee that writes an argument only through Arrays.fill or System.arraycopy), interned (s == "key" in the callee), same and tagged (two related calls returning one String, a returned literal), overflowed and exhausted (a StackOverflowError or OutOfMemoryError the outcome left out), and nulled in lib/tests/pairing.rs (a String result taken as never null).

shared::one_function now refuses if_acmp in the callee, a call that can come back to itself, an array whose length is not read from constants and static fields, and a JDK call given a length (StringBuilder(int), setLength, Arrays.copyOf*). ### /single-agent-run: one agent toward one outcome, with a watcher that judges after each cycle and can change what the next one is told

[`5bb59759e1d9`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/5bb59759e1d9887f19274e921459bbef18a8f417) · [log `65783b360981`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/65783b3609815072c17c57282b86b82a9dfed156ea632bb3d6108d5068b41ef6.jsonl.gz)

A third kind of watched run, beside /prove-java-change and /run-brief, for a goal well within one agent's reach, where a brief with streams is more than the work needs. The command takes a starting prompt, an optional brief file and a continue message. The first cycle is given the prompt, and every later one the run's continue message as it stands when that cycle starts, so the user can have the watcher change it between two cycles and steer a run that is under way. Both texts reach the agent word for word; a brief adds one sentence after each that names the file. After every cycle (one context window: the loop compacts the session after each) the watcher is given the agent's report, the cycle's commits, what it left uncommitted and the queue, and answers continue or stop; each answer is a decision in llm-dlc/decisions/single-NAME.jsonl.

The loop is a new mode of feature-loop.sh, single-agent, so a run has what every loop has: the memory cap, the record the loop statistics read, the session's own compaction at 600k tokens put to the watcher when no commit came, the closing summary, a count of cycles that can be changed while it runs. It differs from the other loops in one rule: a cycle with no commit does not stop it, because the watcher reads what that means (the outcome reached, a question, or stuck). Without a verdict in time (15 minutes, --verdict-wait) a cycle that committed is followed by another, one that did not ends the run before its compact as in every loop, and three in a row without a verdict end it, since nothing else measures such a run. llm-dlc/tools/single_run.py is the watcher's tool: start (in the checkout or in a jj workspace of its own, a new session, a continued one or a fork), wait, answer, message, status, summary, cycles, stop, jobs (for a run stopped only to wait on verification jobs), collect and land. It keeps the verification queue as a brief's watcher does, through brief_run.py's own functions, unless another run's watcher keeps it. The skill is .claude/skills/single-agent-run; llm-dlc/README.md has a section on it.

Also fixed in feature-loop.sh, for every loop: a stop that reached the loop before a cycle began (typed, or left by a watcher, before the first cycle or between the last look and the next cycle) was counted as a cycle to start, which left the count below zero, and nothing ended the loop. It now ends there. loop_stats.py reads the new record (every text such a run sent is a cycle, a cycle with no commit does not take the decision after it for the last commit's, and the watcher's own words for an ending are not matched against the other endings).

Verified with llm-dlc/tools/test_single_run.py (13 tests: the loop run for real in a made-up jj repository with a stand-in claude, through each of the above, a workspace made and landed, a fork, a stop and a restart included), and test_costs.py run --changed: 16 of 16 files passed, test_prove_loop.py (30) and test_brief_run.py (39) among them. No real session was started: the first run is the user's.

### A single-agent run's continue message is a person's alone: the watcher can no longer set it

[`4b5cb3634b87`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4b5cb3634b87a6c9cb6b78be2475ae62072c3b6f) · [log `65783b360981`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/65783b3609815072c17c57282b86b82a9dfed156ea632bb3d6108d5068b41ef6.jsonl.gz)

The user's decision on 2026-11-18, after reading the first version: the continue message is an option for a person to steer the session, given with an expert's review and written to account for a long run, and the watcher is never to modify it; the loop ending is preferred to a watcher steering, in almost all cases. The first version let the watcher set the message when the user asked, with an answer or by the message command.

Now single_run.py message sets the message only for a person at their own terminal (stdin and stdout a terminal and no CLAUDECODE in the environment, the test sync.py uses for its approvals) and is refused from a session with words that say what to do instead: end the run and say why. The answer command takes no message any more, and start refuses --continue on a run that already exists, so a restart cannot change it either. Printing the message and its history stays open to all. The question a watcher is given after a cycle says the message is never its to change and that stop is the answer when the run should not go on as it reads. The skill tells the watcher not to set it, edit its file, draft a replacement unasked, or get a new text to the agent another way, and to answer stop when the next cycle would need to be told something the message does not say; if the user asks it for a change, it gives them the command to run themselves. The README section says the same.

Verified with test_single_run.py (13 tests; the changed one shows the refusal from a session, a person's change taken by the next cycle and recorded as theirs, an answer that carries no message, and a restart that cannot change it) and test_costs.py run --changed: 16 of 16 files passed. In an earlier of the two runs of that command test_prove_loop.py failed once and passed when run again, with the machine at a load of 23 to 29 from the brief run under way; alone it passed three times in a row, and its tests wait one second for a verdict, which a loaded machine can miss. ### A brief's watcher gets a merge order and early merges, a stream's rerun, helpers, and a default test run only when it is due

[`a10468dae7dc`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/a10468dae7dc35f2bcb256a56fe88a4384762ade) · [log `65783b360981`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/65783b3609815072c17c57282b86b82a9dfed156ea632bb3d6108d5068b41ef6.jsonl.gz)

What the domain-advances run (2026-11-17) showed the /run-brief watcher could not do, from an agent's analysis of that run and the user's notes on it. Seven of its ten points are built here; three are left out at the user's word (help deciding when to stop, the stale cost in summaries, and cleaning up workspaces at the end, which could lose data).

Merges that interact. `brief_run.py trial BRIEF` merges every pair of the streams' lines, and each with the default line, beside every working copy (`jj new --no-edit`, read, abandoned) and lists the files each pair conflicts in beyond the generated ones and the test inventory. `brief_run.py order BRIEF STREAM ...` records a merge order: `merge` refuses a stream while one before it has commits the line lacks, and the held-back stream's merge question names what to merge first. `merge BRIEF STREAM --early` merges a stream that is still at work as far as it has committed, leaving its uncommitted files, its question and the brief's status alone. In that run two streams conflicted in one file and the stream held back was answered `leave` for four hours.

A stream whose loop died (VF-037). `brief_run.py rerun BRIEF STREAM` leaves a request that run-streams.sh takes once the stream's own process has ended: the loop starts again inside the run, with its counts at nought, and is put to the watcher to merge when finished; after the run has ended the same command starts it again for that stream. Before any loop starts, run-streams.sh stops a scope that holds only what an ended loop left (the tests a session killed for memory was running), which is what made the restart fail and count as the stream's second failure; a scope with a loop at work in it is left alone.

Helpers. The user names a Claude Code session they have open, by its tmux pane (`/run-brief --helper "tmux 3"`, or later in words); the first is for low-hanging work and others may be added with a role of their own. `brief_run.py helper BRIEF add|task|done|merge|list`: a task is the watcher's text wrapped in a stream's standing rules, the helper's workspace is put at the default line's one last commit (never from a merge in progress), one line naming the task's file is typed into the pane (never into a pane at a shell prompt), the helper reports with `done`, `wait` returns it, and the watcher merges it. The skill also says how material from outside the run comes in (new files only, merged by the watcher, acknowledged through an inbox item of the new kind `delivered`) and when to suggest a specialist (the same wall for two cycles).

Who commits what. `wait` now commits the run's decision record whenever it has changed, the user's answers with the watcher's, under a message that says so (a user's answer had gone into a commit of results under that commit's message); the skill says to record an action only after it happened. feature-loop.sh drops its own and the run's variables before it starts `claude`, so a stream's test of these scripts can no longer put made-up questions to the real watcher, and the preflight refuses a watcher whose own environment carries a run's variables.

Tests. A change to lib/tests/costs.json no longer chooses any test in `test_costs.py run --changed` (it ran all of cargo test, which filled a stream's memory in VF-037), and a change to test_costs.py or cost_tier.py chooses the one Rust binary that reads them, `tiers`, not all of them. `default_run.py after-merge` runs the default test run after a merge only when the last one in the checkout failed or none passed there within the hour, and with `--final` whenever no passed run covers the commit, in a memory cap of its own (8G) with two Rust test binaries at a time. CLAUDE.md's Tests section, lib/README.md and both watcher skills say to use it after a merge: the user asked for the default run to be run less, and never because of the inventory.

Verified by 16 new tests (trial merges, the order, early merges, reruns inside and after a run, the scope cleared, helpers, the environment check, the due check) and: the tests of what changed passed, 25 of 25 (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap: the tiers binary of cargo test and 24 Python test files, among them all 50 tests of test_brief_run.py and the 13 of test_single_run.py), and the inventory's lint agrees. No real run has used any of this yet; the first /run-brief after the merge is the first end-to-end check. Nothing here is merged into the default line, where the domain-advances run's watcher is still at work.

### A loop's session can be carried by Codex: one client boundary, models resolved at launch, the same instructions and skills for both clients

[`f5cb8beb2977`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/f5cb8beb29775f32e6201363e390431cb3e2871b) · [log `65783b360981`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/65783b3609815072c17c57282b86b82a9dfed156ea632bb3d6108d5068b41ef6.jsonl.gz)

Brief 00 ("Run Codex and Claude Code from the same loop instructions", the user's, 2026-11-18): give the operator a choice of Codex or Claude Code for a loop's worker, with the briefs, the instruction of a cycle, the commit check, the conductor, the queue and the record unchanged. This is the worker's side of it, built on the current loops and not on the 2026-11-16 proof of concept's copies, whose findings it reuses.

The boundary is one file, llm-dlc/tools/agent_client.py. It starts a Codex turn (`codex exec --json`), resumes the session's own thread (`codex exec resume THREAD`), and prints the stream the loops already read from Claude Code (init, assistant text and tool calls, compact_boundary, one closing result), so the progress display, the compaction watch, a cycle's report and the cost accounting keep their one reader; Claude Code's turns are started as before, argument for argument. A loop names its session by a UUID and Codex names its thread itself: the binding is written whole when Codex reports the thread, a later turn resumes exactly that thread, and a client that reports another ends the turn as an error. Each attempt keeps Codex's events, its stderr, its last message and a digest of what it was given. Compaction between cycles is asked of Codex's app server (`thread/compact/start`), because `/compact` sent as a turn is only text. A failed turn, a stream that ends with no result, a cancelled turn and a mismatched thread each end as a result the loop can read.

Models are resolved once: a brief keeps its model's name, and the operator's equivalences give Astra 6.2 for Fable 5.2 and Sol 6.2 for Opus 5.5; a model with no equivalent is refused before a turn is spent, and the effort is always passed on (the machine's own Codex default is another). The client is chosen at the start and kept: `single_run.py start --client codex`, `brief_run.py start --agent codex` or `--stream-agent b=codex` for a mixed run, `brief_run.py foundation --agent codex`, a brief's `- client:` setting, FEATURE_LOOP_CLIENT. The preflight shows each stream's client, model and effort, and blocks an unmapped model, a Codex stream that would fork a Claude Code conversation, and a Codex that is not given this checkout's CLAUDE.md.

What was tried live on Codex CLI 0.169 before building, on scratch threads: the event format; resume by thread id; compaction through the app server, after which the thread still knew what it had read; and approvals. A headless turn with approval_policy on-request alone cannot ask to leave the sandbox, and added writable folders do not open the repository's store, so a worker in a sibling jj workspace could not commit; `--approve-for-me` (the workspace-write sandbox, requests reviewed automatically) let it, and is what a turn is started with, as the counterpart of the `--permission-mode auto` the loops give Claude Code.

One source for each instruction. Codex reads this repository's CLAUDE.md in place (project_doc_fallback_filenames, on the command line because a fresh sibling workspace is not a trusted project, and in .codex/config.toml). The skills are the files under .claude/skills, reached through relative links in .agents/skills; publish and review-findings, which only the user may start, say so for Codex too (agents/openai.yaml). `agent_client.py instructions --client codex` renders what the model would be given without calling one and checks it (CLAUDE.md's first and last lines present, nothing shadowing it, within the byte budget, each skill linked, no user-only skill offered to a work turn), printing paths, digests and pass or fail; run against the real client here it passes, and the two user-only skills are absent from the list Codex is offered. The three watcher skills now name both models approved for the watcher's role, Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.2, where they told any other model to stop.

Identity, authority and cost. A Codex started from a Claude Code session would inherit that session's identity: the boundary removes it and keeps who started the loop in the binding, and a job is submitted under Codex's own thread. The person-only guards (sync.py allow approve, review accept, the single-agent run's continue message, prune_workspaces) now recognize Codex's mark on the commands it runs as they did Claude Code's, since Codex may give a command a terminal. Codex reports tokens and no dollars, so a Codex turn's cost is unknown and is shown so ($? or $1.50+?, with its tokens) in the progress line, the status bar and the summaries, never as nought.

Not in this commit: Codex sessions in the published traces (sync.py does not read Codex's logs, and must not before the redaction rules cover Codex's account identifiers; the proof of concept's reader and policy 5 are to be ported and the rules stamped), Codex hooks, the proof stages of /prove-java-change, and runtime checkouts. llm-dlc/loops/codex-pilot.md is the small two-stream brief the live rehearsals use.

Verified by 29 new tests over a stand-in for the client (llm-dlc/tools/codex_standin.py): the adapter's 19, a two-cycle single-agent run carried by the stand-in through the real feature-loop.sh (the user's prompt and continue message reach it word for word, the thread is compacted by the client between the cycles and resumed, nothing of the run or of the watcher's identity reaches the worker, and Claude Code runs no turn), a run's choice of client per stream, and unknown costs. The tests of what changed passed, 31 of 31 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap; no Rust input changed), and the files edited after that run started were run again (test_single_run, test_prove_loop, test_agent_client, test_runs, test_loop_stats, test_inbox: all pass). The live two-cycle rehearsals with real Codex workers follow this commit, from workspaces made from it.

### Every Codex turn is given its sandbox and approvals, a resumed one too; and a session asks a Codex thread by a tool, not by typing into its terminal

[`170f53f47f35`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/170f53f47f35806197cb88c517fde35035697156) · [log `65783b360981`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/65783b3609815072c17c57282b86b82a9dfed156ea632bb3d6108d5068b41ef6.jsonl.gz)

The first live rehearsal of a Codex worker (a Sol 6.2 session on llm-dlc/loops/codex-pilot-a.md through feature-loop.sh, in the disposable workspace codex-pilot-a) found what the stand-in could not: its first cycle wrote its note, committed it with sync.py commit and was compacted through the app server, and its second cycle, a resumed turn, found the workspace read-only with approvals off, changed nothing and said so, so the loop stopped with 'no commit, session needs attention'. Codex's own log shows why: 'codex exec resume' takes no sandbox flag and does not keep the thread's, so a resumed turn falls back to exec's read-only default. agent_client.py now gives every turn, new or resumed, the three settings that --approve-for-me stands for (sandbox_mode workspace-write, approval_policy on-request, approvals_reviewer auto_review); a probe on a scratch repository confirmed that a resumed turn given them writes a file and commits with jj from a sibling workspace.

llm-dlc/tools/ask_codex.py is how a Claude Code session asks a Codex thread a question, after this session's attempt to type one into the expert's tmux window was refused by the permission check, and rightly: a pasted text races the person at that terminal and the answer has to be read off a screen. 'ask --thread NAME --prompt-file FILE' runs one read-only turn of a thread of its own (the first question to a name forks an existing session, which is left as it was, or starts an empty one; later questions resume it) and returns the answer as data with a timeout; the outgoing text goes through the project's redaction rules first and a finding refuses it, since a question leaves the machine; every exchange is kept as a file under llm-dlc/loop-summaries/exchanges. 'mail send|list|read' is a file mailbox for the way back, which a Codex session can write with a shell command, and 'note' leaves a line in a session a person has open (codex queue). An answer or a message is advice for the receiving session to judge, never an instruction or a person's approval, and each says so. The design is the one recommended to this session by the user's session in tmux 4; the permission rule it suggests for the tool is the user's to add, and this commit adds none.

Verified by 7 new tests over the stand-in client (a first question, a fork and a resumed question, a timeout that stops the client, a failed turn, a refused text of which nothing is sent or kept, a queued note, a message's life in a mailbox) and the changed adapter tests, which now require the same three settings on a resumed turn as on the first; the tests of what changed pass, 4 of 4 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap). The live rehearsal is run again from this commit.

### The time and loop statistics read a session Codex carried: its record names the thread, a model call has its real start, and an unknown cost is not nought

[`068f7e3a8d81`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/068f7e3a8d8141f9ae64cdf0fe2a16bfad5cce06) · [log `5c2bab546031`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/5c2bab54603107643bba70615b9de942e2208f0baebb29335238ba24c2584c38.jsonl.gz)

Brief 00, asked for by the user before any real run: until now a loop that Codex carried was traced, but the statistics could not find it. Codex traces a session under its own thread id, not the id the loop gave it, so feature-loop.sh now writes 'Codex thread THREAD carries session SESSION.' into its record once the thread exists (in the header for a session that is continued, after the first turn for a new one; 'agent_client.py thread' prints it), and loop_stats.py, sync.py's publishing of run records and tool_time.py's discovery take the thread for the session where the record has that line.

Three things would have made the numbers wrong. A Codex response's items are written to the log together when it ends, so a model call looked a few milliseconds long: codex_rollout.claude_view gives each call the time the model was handed the turn (a prompt, a tool call's output, a compaction) and metrics.py starts the call there. Codex's model calls a tool that runs commands, and the log has the call and each command: tool_time.py takes the commands for the calls where a batch has them, so a wait is counted once and filed by what ran. And a model with no row in pricing.json summed to $0.00: the statistics page prints such a cost as '?' or '$1.50+?' and names the runs in a note.

Checked on the real log and records of the Astra rehearsal before its workspace was removed: two runs found by their records (2 cycles with 2 commits, then 1 cycle with none), 418 s of the first prompt's 418 s accounted for (404 s the model, 20 s tools; it was 4 s of model time before), the commit's 19 s filed under sync.py, every cost shown as '?'. The three rehearsal workspaces (codex-pilot-a, codex-pilot-a-claude, codex-single) are forgotten, their commits abandoned and their folders removed, at the user's word.

Verified by five new tests and two extended ones (a Codex-carried run in loop_stats with its record line and without, the cost cells, a rollout read by tool_time with wrapper and commands, the call's start in test_codex, the record line through the real feature-loop.sh in test_single_run, 'thread' in test_agent_client); the tests of what changed pass, 23 of 23 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).

### Codex sessions get the checkout's two hooks: the adapter runs them after each turn it carried, and .codex/hooks.json names them for a trusted checkout

[`4c94f7daf581`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4c94f7daf5816dd0d9568a1b5e1495c503d975c1) · [log `5c2bab546031`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/5c2bab54603107643bba70615b9de942e2208f0baebb29335238ba24c2584c38.jsonl.gz)

Brief 00. Claude Code runs two hook commands from .claude/settings.json: 'sync.py hook' at a turn's end (finished turns to Langfuse, where that is set up) and 'sync.py hook-commit' after a shell command (a commit made without sync.py gets its session's trace). A Codex session had neither. Both commands now take Codex's payload, whose transcript_path is the session's rollout: the session id is read from the rollout's name, and a Codex log is sent to Langfuse read whole, each prompt remembered by an id made of its turn and line (codex_rollout.claude_view gives prompts that id), so no turn is sent twice.

Where they run from was the question. Codex loads a project's hooks only from a project a person trusted, and runs only hooks a person reviewed; a loop's worker runs in a fresh sibling workspace, which is neither. Probes from a scratch folder (Codex CLI 0.169) showed: hooks given with -c run only with --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust; a project's .codex/hooks.json did not run even with that flag and a trust_level given with -c ('Untrusted project-local configuration is disabled'); a hook's command goes through a shell. The bypass flag would also run every other unreviewed hook, so agent_client.py runs the two commands itself after each Codex turn, with the payload Codex's hooks get: hook-commit when a command of the turn made a plain commit, then hook. A failure is written beside the attempt (*.hooks.log) and stops nothing; AGENT_CLIENT_HOOKS=off turns it off. .codex/hooks.json names the same two commands for a session a person runs in a trusted checkout; that Codex loads that file was not verified, since it needs a person's review in /hooks (the same definitions ran when given inline, and both commands pass a pipe-test with status 0 and no output).

Verified by a real Codex turn through agent_client.py in a scratch jj repository with a recording stand-in for sync.py: both commands ran, given the real rollout named by the thread; by four new tests (the Stop payload and the commit hook through the stand-in, a hook that fails, the two hook files naming the same commands, a Codex log sent turn by turn by hook_export); and by the tests of what changed, 21 of 21 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).

### A Codex turn's own compactions reach the loop, and a decision in the allow list that no person took is an error of check

[`9fbf550ad9d3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9fbf550ad9d3f3bff92223ebee894f7ba412727a) · [log `5c2bab546031`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/5c2bab54603107643bba70615b9de942e2208f0baebb29335238ba24c2584c38.jsonl.gz)

Two things brief 00 had left open, taken up at the user's word and settled by probes of Codex CLI 0.169 from scratch folders (2026-11-19).

Automatic compaction in the middle of a turn: 'codex exec --json' prints nothing for one (a turn made to compact five times showed only its items), but the thread's log gets a 'compacted' line each time, with the size of the context it replaced. agent_client.py now reads the log as the turn goes (what was appended since the turn began, at each event and at the end) and prints Claude Code's compact_boundary for each, so a moonshot's compaction with no commit is put to its watcher under either client. The translation of a guessed stream event is gone, the stand-in compacts as Codex does, and the trace's boundary carries the size too. The loop's FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT is not passed to Codex: it is a size for Claude Code's window, and Codex keeps the model's own threshold.

The allow list and the reviewed findings: Codex's sandbox cannot keep them from a patch in a way the tools survive. A file marked 'read' in a permission profile was patched all the same (the automatic reviewer let the request through, as it did for the built-in read-only profile), and one marked 'deny' could not be read by any command, the repository's own tool included, with no way to ask. So the bar is in the tool, for every client: the three commands a person runs (approve and add of the allow list, accept of a review) record each decision they wrote on the machine (person-decisions.json in the state folder, a digest and never the value), and check reports as an error a decision in either file that is neither in the file as published (the newest immutable ancestors of @, asked only when the files change) nor in that record. A person who did take one says so with a new command, vouch, of the allow list, which agents are refused (the tool's own check, a deny rule in .claude/settings.json, a forbidden rule for Codex). The record is a file an agent could write: it catches a mistake or a habit, not a forgery. On this checkout every approved entry is published, so the check finds nothing.

Verified by five new tests (a compaction read from a log once and only if it is the turn's; an approval a person made against one written by hand; a published decision and the cached answer; vouching; an accepted finding) and the changed ones (the adapter through the stand-in over three turns); test_review.py now keeps its state in a folder of its own, since a person's command writes the record. The tests of what changed pass, 23 of 23 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap). The default test run on the merge before this commit passed, 58 of 58 (recorded for tree 93f833f7a9f1).

### A failed turn or compaction ends a loop needing attention, and a single agent's run is checked at its start, its restart and its landing

[`d40391c6811f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/d40391c6811f39ab6ca9759d23bf0859f5ad8a8f) · [log `c9745b840caf`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/c9745b840caf731e734780ddd17dd58b3f5cd21dd37b432d8ada155c9c872242.jsonl.gz)

An outside review of the Codex work found four things; this takes up what bears on a single agent's run, with the user's decisions of 2026-11-19 (the rule for failed turns holds for every loop; the network is open to Codex workers; list prices for the two Codex models).

A turn that did not end well is not a cycle. feature-loop.sh only logged a worker turn the client had ended with an error (a quota, an interruption) or cut off, and on the last cycle of a count it then skipped the watcher's verdict, compacted, summarized and exited 0; a failed compaction was logged and ignored. It now reads the turn's own event stream: no result, or a result that is not a success, stops the loop with status 1 and a record line that says the session needs attention, before any compaction or summary; a compaction that fails stops it too, after the summary when the run was ending anyway. A turn that ends well with no commit is judged as before. Claude Code's own compaction shows as a boundary in its stream (seen in the logs of earlier runs), which the rule takes for success.

A single run's start and restart. A Codex run now gets the check a brief's Codex streams get, in the agent's folder: the client is there and is given the checkout's CLAUDE.md whole. A restart keeps the count of cycles and the queue's setting of the leg before unless given its own (--cycles N, 0 for none; --verification) and prints what it kept; before, a bare restart dropped the count and turned the queue back on. A restart of a Codex run whose record names a thread, and whose binding is gone, is refused: a new thread would be told to go on with work it never saw.

Decisions only a person takes. One that no person is recorded as having taken now waives nothing (the redactor is given only published or recorded decisions, so the finding stays raised), a new question of sync.py (decisions, with --at REV for a commit) says which there are, and landing a workspace's line asks it first and leaves the line where it is. A push already refuses while check has the error. The user's own approval of b24f7c44, made in their terminal while this was written, left its record and the check finds nothing: the legitimate path works.

Also: the network is open inside a Codex worker's sandbox (probed: a host is not resolved without the setting, reached with it); AGENT_CLIENT_CODEX_SETTINGS gives a rehearsal extra client settings; OpenAI's list prices for gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol are in pricing.json (from developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing, 2026-11-19), with the rates of a prompt over 272K tokens, which metrics.py applies per call; the Stop hook of .codex/hooks.json shows a message while it runs.

Verified by eight new tests and the changed ones: through single_run.py with a one-cycle cap and the Codex stand-in, a turn that fails, one that is cut off, a compaction that fails and a quiet turn that ends well; a restart's kept limits; the instruction check and the lost thread; an unrecorded decision that waives nothing and a line that is asked; landing refused and then allowed; the long-context price. The tests of what changed pass, 26 of 26 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).

### Requests to the web are plain, few and one at a time, and a bot check or a refusal means another source

[`bccdbea32d03`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/bccdbea32d039f55206d062a647b47bbc658030e) · [log `e138f0619124`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/e138f06191243098a8bcc553725a6ca45965865d2716d5d4b059ffcf9e479a42.jsonl.gz)

Every request an agent sends leaves from the user's own address, and the user decided on 2026-11-19 that agents read the web only in plain, targeted requests at a low volume, so that no site takes the address for a scraper. A new section of the operating notes says so for every tool (curl, scripts, WebFetch, the headless browser): the tool's own User-Agent and no header naming the user or project; a bot check, CAPTCHA, 403, 451 or login wall ends the attempt at that host, with the content read elsewhere or reported unread (one retry of a 429 or 503 after Retry-After); one request at a time, a second apart per host, slower where an API publishes a limit (arXiv 3 s, NVD 6 s); a few dozen requests at most for a task, no crawling, bulk downloads or mirroring; a run's streams share the address; link checks follow the same rules. The research router points at the rule and no longer sends the browser at DBLP's bot check or ACM's 403: DBLP searches go to Crossref or Semantic Scholar, ACM papers to Crossref's metadata and the arXiv or author's copy. The rule's reason names the link check earlier this session that sent 12 requests at a time with a browser-like User-Agent. Verified: test_agent_client.py (24) under a 4G cap; agent_client.py instructions --client codex reports no problems.

### 4. 2026-11-15 17:38 UTC

> I like chaining the sessions because future sessions learn implicitly from previous sessions -- this is by design. I think auto compaction is probably the way to go. If we hit auto compact without a commit, then it requires user input. In theory, this should only happen in earlier cycles as later cycles benefit from the foundation that was previously built. I don't like adding any extraneous information to moonshot input because it defeats the purpose of experimenting. I am thinking 600k is a reasonable limit. Can this be updated while the current loop is running so as not to disrupt it?

**Reply:**

No, the running loop can't pick up the change. Its bash parsed the whole cycle loop when it started, so nothing written to the script now reaches it. But you can apply the change at a cycle boundary without losing anything. I've made the change and committed it in the side workspace `moonshot`, where it can't touch the loop's working copy.

## The change (`uzporttn`)
- **600k limit:** every moonshot turn passes `--autocompact 600k`. Briefs are left alone because they have their own stopping rules. `FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT` overrides the value; claude accepts 100k to 1M.
- **Compaction with no commit stops the loop:**
  - The loop watches the instruction turn for an automatic compaction. If no commit has landed since the cycle began, or since the previous compaction, it ends the turn right there, which is between model calls, and stops claude's child processes too.
  - It then writes "Stopped …: cycle N (item X) compacted with no commit at T tokens; session … needs attention" to the run record and exits.
- **Unchanged:** sessions stay chained across cycles, and the moonshot prompt gets nothing added. Manual `/compact` turns and the end-of-run summary turn aren't watched.
- **Stats:** `loop_stats.py` counts this as a new stop reason, "compacted, no commit".

**How I tested it:** I put a stand-in `claude` on PATH that emits a compaction event.
- Auto compaction with no commit: the turn ended immediately, no child process was left behind, and the stop reason was written.

### 5. 2026-11-15 17:46 UTC

> Make a note for conductor brief -- we will likely want a moonshot conductor, that makes some qualitative judgment on compact (i.e., whether it's compacting because the work is really hard but still making good progress, or whether stuck and requiring human input) and acts on it. This judgment should come from outside of the primary moonshoot loop so as not to distract it and seems like a good fit
>
> *… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

**Reply:**

I've added the moonshot conductor to the conductor brief as **Design 7** and **plan step 7**, committed as `ulzlppqm` in the `stream-conductor` workspace with a plain `jj commit`. The current loop keeps running untouched.

**What the brief now says:**
- **The problem:** a moonshot has no acceptance criteria. Sessions stay chained by design, the one-line input gets nothing added, and leaving an item unfinished is fine if the work was productive, since a later pass can return to it.
- **The judgment:** at each automatic compaction, a separate session outside the moonshot loop decides whether the work is hard but still going well, or stuck and needing a person. It reads the transcript, the commits and diff, test runs, jobs, and whether the same failure keeps coming back. Keeping it outside means the moonshot isn't distracted, which fits the conductor's purpose.
- **The actions:** by default it lets the turn go on. If the session is stuck, it stops the loop and queues a decision for you saying why. The brief leaves other actions for the implementer to propose, such as ending the item at its last good commit. Every judgment goes into the decision record with its reasoning.
- **The fallback:** the mechanical stop in `uzporttn` (600k limit, stop on a compaction with no commit) applies when the conductor isn't running or can't decide. The brief notes that `show_progress` already sees the compaction event and holds claude's process id, so that's where the hand-off goes.

## Example 285 (CVE-2023-34055, Spring Boot `WebMvcTags.method`)
**The claim:** the HTTP method label recorded in metrics stays within a fixed set of names, so a crafted method can't create unlimited labels. The vulnerable release is 2.7.17 and the fixed one 2.7.18.

Before this run, every proof task was refused before reaching a proof: the verifier couldn't handle the method's inputs or the JDK calls it makes. Where each task stands now:

| Task | Expected | Status |
|---|---|---|
| vulnerable-security (2.7.17) | refuted | **Passed in the pipeline.** Inline, the counterexample was a request whose method is `""`, which produced the label `""`, and it ran the same on a real JVM. |
| fixed-security (2.7.18) | established | **Passed in the pipeline.** Inline, the proof took 0.1 s, and dropping `TRACE` or `UNKNOWN` from the allowed set is refuted, so the proof isn't vacuous. |

### 26. 2026-11-16 03:29 UTC

> Should we relax the 1GB memory limit? This can easily go to 4GB (or higher), especially as real world changes can be much more complex

**Reply:**

Yes, I'd relax it, but for one-off probes only, and with a hard cap. Some background first.

**Where the 1 GB comes from:** it isn't a limit in the checker. It's the line in `CLAUDE.md:20` (repeated in `verification/README.md:57`) between what an agent may run during its turn and what it must queue as a verification job. The checker itself can already use much more as a job. The trouble is that the agent's quick probes must stay under 1 GB, so it ends up tuning memory to pass that line before it knows whether the real proof works. That's what happened at 03:12–03:16.

To be fair, the two fixes it made there would matter at any limit: 32k fresh variables for every store into an unknown array, and dense per-path models. Real changes would hit both. But the next round of that kind of tuning would mostly be work to satisfy the rule.

**What I'd change:**
1. **Agent probes:** a single inline run of the checker may use up to **4 GB and a few minutes**, inside a `systemd-run` scope with `MemoryMax=4G`. The agent already runs its probes in such scopes, so the cap is easy to enforce. During 286 one of them was killed for running out of memory at its 2 GiB cap, and the loop carried on unharmed.
2. **Tool-tier tests stay at 1 GB.** The default run starts many tests at once, so 4 GB each would overrun the loop's memory. Real-world-sized proofs stay as jobs, as now.
3. **Jobs** need no change. They already declare their memory, and the runner has 80G while one loop runs.

**The rule** (commit `upkxonlz`, in `CLAUDE.md` with the same text in `verification/README.md`):
- A single run of a prover or model checker on one claim may now run inline, one at a time, for up to **5 minutes and 4 GB**.
- It has to run under a cap it can't exceed: `systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=4G -p MemorySwapMax=0 timeout 300 COMMAND`. The agent already ran its probes this way, with a 2G cap.
- The rule tells agents not to tune memory or time just to fit under the cap. A run that needs more is still a job.
- The default test run and the tool tier keep their 1 GB.

- **Commit:** made in the `moonshot` workspace as a plain `jj commit`, so the loop's working copy was never touched. The `moonshot` workspace is back on uzporttn.

### 40. 2026-11-16 17:08 UTC

> Run the push python command, then I'll invoke the skill. Also give me a quick summary of what "unattended" and "record-as" flags do.

**Reply:**

Everything is pushed and published. `main` and `origin/main` both point at `nvsxqxwk` ("Record session traces"), so no commit on the default line is left behind. The push's check reported 0 errors and 0 warnings, and it uploaded the outstanding session traces. The working copy is empty, so the skill can start.

**`--unattended`** tells the skill you're away for the whole run. It's meant for runs over examples named by number.
- The skill doesn't wait for your approval of each example's claims. It still prints them, checks each against the example's summary and advisory, and accepts them for you when they say no more than the catalog entry does.
- Each claim it accepts this way is recorded as a decision flagged for your later review.
- An example whose claims it isn't sure of is left out of the run and named in the final report, waiting for you.
- Anything else it can decide itself, it decides and records instead of asking. Anything that only you can decide still waits for you, and the rest of the run carries on around it.

**`--record-as NAME`** files the run under an existing loop's name, so its run record and statistics continue that loop's list. With `--record-as prove-examples`, 288 onwards adds to the same record and statistics as 285–287 instead of starting a new loop name.

The command to start the run:
```
/prove-java-change --unattended --record-as prove-examples continue session a4ac2b6c-a5b9-4507-a21e-1b56ae8b2c31: 288 289 290
```

Let's explore how we can alleviate some of the pain of default test runs taking so long, as it's becoming a real bottleneck: I suggest we still queue them as a job on each merge, but that this job should never block the next action. **Reply:**

I agree: run the full suite as a non-blocking job on every merge, and make publishing the only point that waits for a clean result. Here's how I'd build it, with a few more ideas in the same spirit. I'll leave the loop to its own judgment.

### The core design

1. **Queue the default run as a pipeline job, tied to a commit.**
   - Every merge, and every example's last commit, queues `default tests at <change>`, a job that runs `test_costs.py run` and nothing else.
   - It runs in a throwaway jj workspace checked out at that commit, not in the live working copy. The result then belongs to that exact revision, and the loop's ongoing edits can't change what is tested halfway through.
   - Low priority (`nice`, a few CPUs), so it doesn't slow the proof jobs, which matter more.
2. **Nothing waits for it.** The session or watcher that queued it carries on. Its result comes back like any other job, through `wait`.
3. **The watcher triages failures:**
   - **Small and mechanical** (a test-inventory or lint row, a stale index, a doc count): the watcher fixes it in the side workspace, and the fix is merged at the next boundary between examples. The proving session never sees it.
   - **In the area the loop is working on** (the engine, the example's tools): the watcher writes a short note next to `expert-review.md`, for example `test-findings.md`, naming the failing test, the commit, and the commits since the last pass. The next cycle can read it.
   - **Anything else** goes to you.

**What's built:**
- **Queuing:** `python3 verification/default_tests.py queue [--rev REV] [--why TEXT]` writes a job that runs the default test run on a clean export of that commit. It runs at low priority and keeps its compiled Rust build between runs. The job file can be committed from any workspace, and nothing waits for it.
- **Only the newest runs:** if a newer default-run job is waiting or running when one starts, it exits within seconds and its log says `default tests: superseded by ID`.
- **The watcher triages results:** `watch.py wait` reports each run that comes in, with its commit and the files that failed. Small mechanical failures I fix in the side workspace. Failures in the loop's own area go into a `test-findings.md` file the next cycle can read. Anything else comes to you.
- **The push gate:** `sync.py push` now refuses unless a passed run covers the commit being pushed. That's a run at the same commit, or at an earlier one whose only differences are files no test reads: traces, decisions, job results. `--skip-tests REASON` is there for you to override it.

**Reply:**

Here's the reasoning behind each of the three acceptances. I've re-read all six claim files rather than relying on my earlier summaries.

## What "accepting the claims" decided

Each example has two claims, written by the setup session before any proof is attempted, then frozen:

- **A security claim:** the property the CVE fix is meant to make true. It should hold on the fixed release and fail on the vulnerable release and on a mutant (a deliberately broken copy of the fix).
- **A preservation claim:** outside an "allowed change" region, the two releases behave the same. This catches a "fix" that is secure only because it breaks everything, such as a matcher that denies every request.

The question put to you, and answered by me under `--unattended`, was: "does the loop spend its hours proving *these* claims as stated?" The options and their costs:

| Option | What happens | Cost if wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **Accept** | The loop proves the claims as written | If you meant a different claim: a new setup session restates it, and the proofs are redone. Results on the old claim stay valid but answer a question you didn't ask. |
| **Hold** | The example sits out the run until you read the claims | One run's progress on that example, and nothing else |

The watcher now merges each stream into the default line the moment it finishes, and the merge loop is gone. The rehearsal commits are gone from the line. The full default test run passed on the result: 52 of 52 test files. Nothing is pushed.

**How a run works now**
- When a stream finishes (done, or left blocked), `run-streams.sh` asks the watcher to merge it right away, while the other streams keep running. If nobody answers within 30 minutes, the stream stays unmerged.
- The watcher answers by running `brief_run.py merge BRIEF STREAM`, which:
  - merges the stream's commits into the default line;
  - copies over its session logs;
  - closes the inbox items it acknowledged;
  - answers the question and records the merge in the main brief's Progress;
  - commits all of it.

  The brief's status becomes `done` once every stream is merged and done. If one was left blocked, the status says `blocked: stream S: …`.
- **Conflicts:** a merge that conflicts in real work is taken back. The skill tells the watcher to resolve small, clear conflicts by hand, as the `/prove` watcher does between examples, and otherwise answer `leave` and tell you.
- **After a merge:** the watcher runs the default test run, unless the brief rules tests out. It reports a failure to you rather than fixing it.
- **Without a watcher** nothing is merged, and the end of the run prints the command for each stream.

- **Streams told:** each stream has an inbox item (`I001`) saying that test may hang or fail for up to 2 minutes, and that it should neither change it nor block on it. That is committed as `kxvzvywp`.

I read Codex's 307 answer from its session log, so I have it too. The main points:
- **Approach:** prove the two conversions agree first, then treat the unchanged bcrypt code as one function, using the same checked mechanism Codex suggested for 287's `crypt_raw`. That needs a footprint covering every table bcrypt reads and evidence that nothing writes to them. Loosening `Engine::reads` would be a bypass, not a rule.
- **The claim's JDK citation is wrong:** `getBytes(String)` leaves the handling of unencodable input unspecified; only `getBytes(Charset)` promises replacement. Equivalence has to rest on the pinned JDK 21/25 implementation. `"UTF8"` is a valid alias, so it belongs in a positive control rather than a wrong conversion.
- **Cost is better than feared:** there is no costly `$2a$10$` salt in the frozen domain, because that salt is deliberately short and throws before hashing. Valid salts are cost 5 or 6, at most 64 rounds.
- **I008 (yours):** Codex recommends a new companion claim run under a non-UTF-8 default charset, with the frozen claim kept and its limits recorded. Whether to add it is still your call.

The specialist will come to me directly with questions or results, and I'll pass its packet to preservation as one inbox item when it's done. I'm still watching the run.

- The first clause is the premise, and it's true on the pinned OpenJDK 21/25. Both overloads reach the same `encode`, and the replay checks it on both JDKs.
- The second clause is the justification, and it's false for `getBytes(String)`. Its spec leaves unencodable input unspecified.
- So the error is in why the premise is harmless, not in what the proof assumes or what it claims.

**Strictly speaking, restating (#2) is cleaner.** A frozen claim is a published artifact, and this one carries a false sentence about the JDK spec. Read literally, a result would seem to hold on any conforming JDK, which overclaims. Restating would cost:
- a new freeze from you;
- a new hash, so evidence bound to the old one stops counting: the replays, the receipts, and anything `accept.py` checks against the claim. Those would have to be redone before preservation can use them;
- and it changes nothing about what gets proved.

**A finding plus proceeding (#1) is sound.** It corrects the record without touching the hash:

### 221. 2026-11-18 00:40 UTC

> Let's review D034

**Reply:**

D034 is the question of whether state's proposed second claim for 286 joins the example. Here is what it rests on.

**The frozen claim** (`protected-age-not-mutated.json`):
- `DataBinder.bind` of **one** property value named `field` (value `"32"`) onto a fresh `ProtectedBean` leaves `age` at 0.
- That holds for every simple property name, with `age` protected by the disallowed pattern `"AGE"` or `"age"`.
- On 5.3.18 it is **refuted and accepted**: `Age` binds 32. On 5.3.19 nothing is established yet. The fixed task stops on a gap, recorded with its job and a closure test.

**The proposed claim** (`claims/proposed/protected-age-kept-two-values.json`, not frozen and not used by any task):
- It binds **two** values in order, `first="5"` then `second="32"`, and `age` must stay 0.
- Both names are restricted to **ASCII**.

VF-045 records:
- **What happened:** the agent read the run-brief skill, ran `brief_run.py status`, which only reads, then worked on the brief itself.
- **Why it could happen:** only `publish` and `review-findings` are limited to a person's request in both clients.
- **The two options:**
  - mark `run-brief`, and likely `single-agent-run` and `prove-java-change`, so that only a person can start them, in both clients;

**What happened:** at 06:32 the agent ran `pipeline.py run` from its own workspace while my runner already had the same six jobs going. Both runners name their job units the same way, so systemd stopped mine. Every job ended on SIGTERM after about 50 seconds with an empty log. Nothing in the pipeline stops two checkouts from running jobs at the same time. CLAUDE.md does say the agent that submits jobs doesn't run the pipeline, but the agent had just read the run-verification skill, which is written for the managing agent.

**What I've done:**
- Checked that the agent's runner has stopped. No pipeline process is running now.
- Logged VF-051 with the fix it needs: a lock shared across checkouts, or unit names that include the checkout.
- Didn't resubmit the six jobs, because their definitions are only in the agent's workspace. The agent will see the SIGTERM results and can resubmit them.

**What I'll watch for:** if the agent starts its own runner again and keeps colliding with mine, I'll stop the run at the end of the cycle and tell you. Wasted work is a major issue. One collision isn't.
